title: Types of Soil
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Earth and space
summary: Sandy, clay and loamy soils — what soil is made of, how to classify and test it, and how changes to soil can help or harm plants, with a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that there are different types of soil, and that soils can be classified (sorted) by how much clay, sand and organic matter (humus) they contain (6ESp.03).
Know that the make-up of a soil can change, and that these changes can help or harm plant growth (6ESp.04).
Skills used on this page: fair testing (drainage test), observing (jar test), recording results in a table, drawing and reading a bar chart, making a conclusion.

blocks.text: Key words

items: soil
تربة — the loose top layer of the ground that plants grow in
particle
جسيم / حبيبة — a very small piece
sand
رمل — the largest soil particles; feel gritty
silt
طمي — medium-sized particles; feel smooth and silky
clay
طين — the smallest particles; sticky when wet
organic matter / humus
مادة عضوية / دُبال — dark material made from dead plants and animals that have rotted (decayed)
loam
تربة طميية (مخلوطة) — a mixture of sand, silt, clay and humus; good for most plants
drain / drainage
تصريف — how quickly water passes through the soil
waterlogged
مشبّعة بالماء — so full of water that there is no air for the roots
nutrients (minerals)
عناصر غذائية / أملاح معدنية — substances in soil that plants need to grow healthily
fertiliser / compost
سماد / سماد عضوي (كومبوست) — added to soil to give it more nutrients or organic matter
erosion
تعرية / انجراف — soil being carried away by wind or water

blocks.text: 1. What is soil made of?
Soil looks simple, but it is a **mixture** of several things:

rows: Rock particles (sand, silt, clay)
Rock broken down into small pieces by the weather over a very long time
Hold the roots in place; the size of the particles controls drainage
Organic matter (humus)
Dead leaves, roots, animals and animal waste that have rotted
Gives nutrients; helps soil hold water; dark colour
Water
Rain and irrigation
Plants take in water through their roots
Air
Fills the spaces between the particles
Roots need oxygen from the air in the soil
Living things
Earthworms, insects, bacteria, fungi
Break down dead material into humus; worms mix the soil and make tunnels

blocks.text: 2. Sand, silt and clay — the particle sizes
Soil scientists sort the rock particles in soil by **size**. The size of the particles changes how the soil feels and how water moves through it.

rows: Sand
Largest — about 0.05 mm to 2 mm; you can see single grains
Gritty and rough; falls apart
Silt
Medium — too small to see single grains
Smooth and silky, like flour
Clay
Smallest — less than 0.002 mm
Sticky when wet; can be rolled and shaped; hard and cracked when dry

blocks.text: 3. Types of soil
Soils are **classified** (sorted into types) by how much **clay**, **sand** and **organic matter** they contain.

rows: Sandy soil
Mostly sand; little clay or humus
Water drains away very quickly; lots of air; dries out fast
Few — nutrients are washed out by the water
Plants that need little water, e.g. cactus, date palms; root crops like carrots
Clay soil
Mostly clay
Water drains very slowly; little air; can become waterlogged; cracks when dry
Many — but roots find it hard to push through
Plants with strong roots; rice; becomes very good when organic matter is added
Loam (loamy soil)
A balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay with plenty of humus
Holds enough water but still drains; plenty of air
Many
Most crops and garden plants — the best soil for farming
Peaty soil
A very high amount of organic matter
Holds a lot of water
Can be poor because the soil is acidic
Some plants that like wet, acidic soil

blocks.text: **Why do sand and clay behave so differently?** Sand grains are large, so the **spaces between them are large** — water runs straight through and air can get in. Clay particles are tiny and pack **tightly together**, so the spaces are tiny — water moves through very slowly and gets trapped.

blocks.alt: Dry soil cracked into many flat plates
blocks.caption: Soil with a lot of clay shrinks and cracks into hard plates when it dries out; when it is wet it becomes sticky and drains slowly.

blocks.title: Egypt connection
blocks.text: The farmland of the **Nile Valley and Delta** is dark soil rich in **silt and clay** that the river carried and left behind over thousands of years — the ancient Egyptians called their land 'Kemet', the black land. Away from the river, most of Egypt is **sandy desert soil**, which drains quickly and has few nutrients.

blocks.alt: Satellite view of Egypt with a green strip along the Nile and a green Delta in sandy desert
blocks.caption: Egypt from space: the green farmland of the Nile Valley and Delta grows on dark silt left by the river, while the land on either side is sandy desert.

blocks.text: 4. Testing soils

**Test 1 — the feel test.** Take a little damp soil and rub it between your fingers. Gritty → mostly sand. Smooth and silky → mostly silt. Sticky, and can be rolled into a long thin sausage → mostly clay.
**Test 2 — the jar test (observing).** This test separates the parts of the soil so you can see how much of each the soil contains.

items: Put soil in a clear jar until it is about one-third full.
Add water until the jar is nearly full, put the lid on and shake it well.
Leave it to settle for a day without moving it.
Observe the layers. The **heaviest, largest** particles settle first at the bottom; the **smallest** (clay) settle last on top. Organic matter (humus) is light and **floats**.

blocks.text: The **thickness** of each layer tells you how much of that particle the soil contains. A thick sand layer → sandy soil; a thick clay layer → clay soil.
**Test 3 — the drainage test (fair test).** Which soil lets water drain through fastest?

blocks.text: **Conclusion:** sandy soil drains fastest because its large particles have large spaces between them; clay soil drains slowest and holds the most water because its tiny particles are tightly packed. To make the results more reliable, repeat each test three times and find the mean.
5. Soil can change
The make-up (composition) of a soil is not fixed. Living things, people and the weather can all change it. Some changes **support** (help) plant growth and some **hinder** (harm) it.

rows: Adding compost or animal manure
More organic matter and nutrients; sandy soil holds more water; clay soil becomes more open and drains better
Supports growth
Leaves and dead animals rot into the soil
More humus and nutrients
Supports growth
Earthworms
Mix the layers, pull leaves down, make tunnels for air and water
Supports growth
Adding sand to heavy clay soil
Larger spaces, better drainage and more air
Supports growth
Adding fertiliser
Replaces the nutrients that crops have used
Supports growth (too much can harm living things)
A river flood leaves silt on the fields
Adds fine, nutrient-rich particles
Supports growth
Growing crops year after year without adding anything
Nutrients are used up and removed with the harvest
Hinders growth
Erosion by wind or heavy rain
The fertile top layer of soil is blown or washed away
Hinders growth
Too much salt (e.g. irrigation water evaporates and leaves salt behind)
The soil becomes salty
Hinders growth — roots find it hard to take in water
Heavy machines or many feet pressing the ground
Soil is squashed (compacted); fewer air spaces; poor drainage
Hinders growth
Pollution (oil, chemicals, rubbish)
Harmful substances in the soil
Hinders growth; can kill soil organisms

blocks.title: Science in Egypt
blocks.text: For thousands of years the Nile flooded every summer and left a fresh layer of fertile silt on the fields. Since the **Aswan High Dam** was built, most of the silt is trapped behind the dam in Lake Nasser, so farmers must add **fertiliser** to replace the nutrients. New farms in the desert improve sandy soil by adding **compost** so that it holds more water and nutrients.

blocks.title: الفكرة الأساسية بالعربي
items: التربة خليط من: حبيبات صخور (رمل وطمي وطين) + مادة عضوية (دُبال) + ماء + هواء + كائنات حية.
الرمل حبيباته كبيرة ← الماء بيعدّي بسرعة (صرف سريع) والتربة بتنشف. الطين حبيباته صغيرة جدًا ومتلاصقة ← بيحتفظ بالماء وممكن يغرق الجذور.
التربة الطميية (loam) خليط متوازن + دبال كتير ← أحسن تربة لمعظم النباتات.
التربة ممكن تتغير: الكومبوست والديدان بيحسّنوها، والتعرية والملوحة والتلوث بيضرّوا النبات.

blocks.text: Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Mariam rubs three damp soil samples between her fingers. Sample K feels gritty and falls apart. Sample L feels sticky and can be rolled into a thin sausage. Sample M is dark, crumbly and has bits of rotted leaves in it. Name the type of soil for each sample. [3 marks]

items: K → **sandy soil** (gritty = large sand grains).
L → **clay soil** (sticky and can be shaped = tiny clay particles).
M → a soil with a **lot of organic matter (humus)** — **loam** or **peaty soil** (dark, rotted leaves).

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Use the drainage results above. (a) How much water did the loam hold? [1] (b) Which soil would be best for a cactus? Give a reason. [2]

items: (b) **Sandy soil** (1 mark). It drains quickly so the soil does not stay wet; cacti need little water (1 mark).

blocks.text: Common mistake: subtracting the wrong way round. Water **held** = water **poured in** − water **collected**.
**Worked example 3** — In a jar test, why does sand settle at the bottom and clay settle on top? [2 marks]

items: Sand particles are **larger / heavier**, so they sink fastest (1 mark).
Clay particles are the **smallest / lightest**, so they sink slowest and settle last, on top (1 mark).

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A farmer's field has sandy soil. Her plants often wilt. Explain how adding compost would help. [2 marks]

items: Compost adds **organic matter (humus)**, which **holds water**, so the soil does not dry out so fast (1 mark).
It also adds **nutrients** that the plants need to grow (1 mark).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Youssef plans a drainage test on two soils. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables. [3 marks]

items: Independent: the **type of soil** (1 mark).
Dependent: the **volume of water** that drains through in a set time (or the time for the water to drain) (1 mark).
Control (any two, 1 mark): same mass of soil / same volume of water / same time / same funnel and filter paper.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying clay soil drains fast because it is 'hard'. Clay drains **slowly** because its tiny particles leave tiny spaces.
Thinking sandy soil is rich in nutrients. Water rushing through sandy soil **washes nutrients away**.
Mixing up **sand**, **silt** and **clay** sizes: sand largest, silt medium, clay smallest.
Forgetting the **air** in soil — roots need oxygen, which is why waterlogged soil harms plants.
In the jar test, saying the smallest particles sink first. The **largest** particles settle first, at the bottom.
Calling a drainage test fair without keeping the **mass of soil** and **volume of water** the same.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Classify a soil** from its description, from a jar-test diagram, or from a table of its sand, clay and organic content.
**Investigation questions:** name the variables, suggest how to make the test fair, read a results table, calculate water held (poured in − collected), say which soil drains fastest.
**Graphs:** draw or read a **bar chart** (soil type is a category, so the bars do not touch).
**Explain** a property: always link it to **particle size** and the **spaces** between particles.
**Soil change** questions: say whether a change helps or harms plants **and why** (more nutrients, more water held, less air, nutrients removed…).

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Types of Soil — Practice
blocks.intro: Answer every question, then check your answers. Open questions: compare your answer with the mark scheme and give yourself the marks you earned.

questions.q: Which soil particles are the smallest?
questions.e: Clay particles are the smallest (less than 0.002 mm). Silt is medium and sand is the largest of the three.

questions.q: What is the name of the dark material in soil that is made from dead plants and animals that have rotted?
questions.e: Humus (organic matter) forms when dead leaves, roots and animals decay.

questions.q: Which type of soil lets water drain through the fastest?
questions.e: Sandy soil has large particles with large spaces between them, so water passes through quickly.

questions.q: Why does clay soil often become waterlogged?
c: It contains a lot of air.
Its particles are large and loose.
It has no water in it.
Its particles are tiny and packed tightly, with very small spaces.
questions.e: Tiny, tightly packed clay particles leave only tiny spaces, so water drains very slowly and collects in the soil.

questions.p:
Question 5
Layla tests three soils, A, B and C. She pours 100 ml of water onto 50 g of each soil in a funnel and measures the water collected after 10 minutes.
Soil A: 72 ml collected.   Soil B: 30 ml collected.   Soil C: 55 ml collected.
questions.q: (a) How much water was held by soil B?
questions.e: Water held = poured in − collected = 100 − 30 = 70 ml.

questions.p:
Question 5
Layla tests three soils, A, B and C. She pours 100 ml of water onto 50 g of each soil in a funnel and measures the water collected after 10 minutes.
Soil A: 72 ml collected.   Soil B: 30 ml collected.   Soil C: 55 ml collected.
questions.q: (b) Which soil most likely contains the most clay? Write the letter.
questions.e: Clay drains slowest and holds the most water. Soil B let the least water through (30 ml), so it has the most clay.

questions.q: (c) Which soil is most likely to be sandy soil? Write the letter.
questions.e: Sandy soil drains fastest. Soil A let the most water through (72 ml).

questions.q: (d) Give two things Layla kept the same to make her test fair.
questions.ms: 1 mark each for any two: same mass of soil (50 g); same volume of water (100 ml); same time (10 minutes); same (size of) funnel / filter paper; same starting dryness of soil. Do not accept 'same soil' (soil type is what she changes).
questions.e: From the question: she used 50 g of each soil, 100 ml of water and measured after 10 minutes — any two of these (or same funnel and filter paper).

Question 6
A jar of soil and water was shaken and left for a day. The diagram shows what it looked like.
questions.q: (b) The material at A floats on the water. What is it?
questions.e: Organic matter (humus) is very light, so it floats.

questions.q: A gardener adds compost to heavy clay soil. Explain how this helps her plants grow.
questions.ms: 1 mark: compost adds nutrients / minerals. 1 mark: it opens up / loosens the soil so it drains better / more air reaches the roots / roots can grow through more easily. Accept: adds organic matter / humus for either mark only if linked to a correct effect.
questions.e: Compost adds organic matter, which adds nutrients and opens up the tightly packed clay, so water drains better and more air reaches the roots.

questions.q: Which change to a soil would hinder (harm) plant growth?
questions.e: Salt in the soil makes it hard for roots to take in water. The other three add air, nutrients or organic matter, which help plants.

questions.q: Before the Aswan High Dam was built, the Nile flooded every year and left silt on the fields. Now most of this silt is trapped behind the dam. Explain why farmers by the Nile now use more fertiliser.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the silt (from floods) added nutrients / minerals to the soil every year. 1 mark: without new silt, crops use up the nutrients / nutrients are not replaced, so fertiliser is needed to replace them.
questions.e: The yearly silt brought fresh nutrients. Now no new silt arrives, so the nutrients that crops take out are not replaced naturally; fertiliser replaces them.

questions.q: A 500 g sample of soil is separated. It contains 150 g of sand and 250 g of clay. The rest is organic matter. What is the mass of the organic matter?

blocks.title: Remember
items: Soil = rock particles (sand, silt, clay) + organic matter (humus) + water + air + living things.
Particle size: **sand** largest (gritty), **silt** medium (silky), **clay** smallest (sticky).
**Sandy** soil drains fast, dries out, few nutrients. **Clay** soil drains slowly, holds water, can be waterlogged. **Loam** = balanced mix + humus, best for most plants.
Drainage test: change the soil type; measure water collected; keep mass of soil, volume of water and time the same. Water held = poured in − collected.
Soil can change: compost, humus, worms and silt **support** growth; erosion, used-up nutrients, salt, compaction and pollution **hinder** it.
